citation.title: A Class of Unbiased Estimators of the Average Treatment Effect in Randomized Experiments

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population, design-based potential-outcomes setting (the Neyman-Rubin model): potential outcomes and covariates are fixed and the only randomness is the assignment of units to treatment and control. Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) Section 3, pp. 137-138 (PDF pp. 3-4): 'Define a binary treatment indicator $T_i$ for units $i = 1,2,\ldots,N$ such that $T_i = 1$ when unit $i$ receives the treatment and $T_i = 0$ otherwise. If the stable unit treatment value assumption [16] holds, let $Y_{1i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is exposed to the treatment, and let $Y_{0i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is not exposed to the treatment. The observed outcome $Y_i$ may be expressed as a function of the potential outcomes and the treatment: $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. [1] The causal effect of the treatment on unit $i$, $\tau_i$, is defined as the difference between the two potential outcomes for unit $i$: $\tau_i \equiv Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$. [2] The ATE, denoted by $\Delta$, is defined as the average value of $\tau_i$ for all units $i$. In the Neyman-Rubin model, the only random component is the allocation of units to treatment and control groups.' Eq. [3]: $\Delta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Y_{1i}-Y_{0i})}{N} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right]$, 'where $Y_1^T$ is the sum of the potential outcomes if in the treatment condition and $Y_0^T$ is the sum of potential outcomes if in the control condition.' Eq. [4]: $\widehat{\Delta} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y_1^T} - \widehat{Y_0^T}\right]$, 'where $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ is the estimated sum of potential outcomes under treatment and $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ is the estimated sum of potential outcomes under control.' Footnote 2 (p. 138): 'This assumption is made without loss of generality; multiple discrete treatments (or equivalently, some units not being sampled into either treatment or control) are easily accommodated in this framework. All instances of $(1 - T_i)$ in the text may be replaced by $C_i$, an indicator variable for whether or not unit $i$ receives the control, with one exception to be noted in Section 6.'

(S2) p. 138 (PDF p. 4): 'Formally, the bias of an estimator is the difference between the expected value of the estimator and the true parameter of interest; an estimator is unbiased if this difference is equal to zero. If the estimators $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ and $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ are unbiased, the corresponding estimator of $\Delta$ is also unbiased since $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_1^T}] - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_0^T}]\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right] = \Delta$.' [5]

(S3) Section 4, p. 138 (PDF p. 4): 'Define $N$ as the number of units in the study, $\pi_{1i}$ as the probability that unit $i$ is selected into treatment, and $\pi_{0i}$ as the probability that unit $i$ is selected into control. We assume that, $\forall i$, $\pi_{1i} > 0$ and $\pi_{0i} > 0$, or that there is a nonzero probability that each unit will be selected into treatment and that there is a nonzero probability that each unit will be selected into control. (When all units are assigned to either treatment or control, $\pi_{0i} + \pi_{1i} = 1$.)'

(S4) Section 5, pp. 140-141 (PDF pp. 6-7): eqs. [13]-[14], $\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$ and $\widehat{Y_0^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-T_i)\frac{Y_{0i}}{\pi_{0i}} - (1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$, 'where $f(.)$ is a predetermined real-valued function of pretreatment covariate vector $\mathbf{X_i}$ and of parameter vector $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$'; eq. [15], $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} - \widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right)$; eq. [16], $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$.

(S5) Section 6.1, p. 143 (PDF p. 9): '$\pi_{1i1j}$ is the probability that units $i$ and $j$ are jointly included in the treatment group'; '$\pi_{0i0j}$ is the probability that units $i$ and $j$ are jointly included in the control group'; '$\pi_{1i0j}$ is the joint probability that unit $i$ will be in the treatment group and unit $j$ will be in the control group.'

(S6) Section 6.2, pp. 143-144 (PDF pp. 9-10): 'When $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ is constant, we may simply redefine the outcome variable, $U_i = Y_i - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$. It follows that $U_{0i} = Y_{0i} - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ and $U_{1i} = Y_{1i} - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$.' and 'As we proceed, for notational clarity, we use $Y_i$ as the outcome measure, noting that the variances derived will also apply to the generalized difference estimator if $U_i$ is substituted for $Y_i$ (along with both associated potential outcomes) and $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ is constant.'

(S7) Section 6.3, pp. 144-145 (PDF pp. 10-11), cluster totals: 'Note that if, for some units $i,j$, $\Pr(T_i \neq T_j) = 0$, then the total estimators may be equivalently rewritten. Define $K_k \in \mathbf{K}$ as the set of unit indices $i$ that satisfy $T_i = T'_k$, where $T'_k$ is indexed over all $|\mathbf{K}|$ unique random variables in $\{T_i : i = (1,2,\ldots,N)\}$. Define $\pi'_{1k}$ as the value of $\pi_{1i}, \forall i \in K_k$, $\pi'_{0k}$ as the value of $\pi_{0i}, \forall i \in K_k$. Joint probabilities $\pi'_{1k1l}$, $\pi'_{1k0l}$, and $\pi'_{0k0l}$ are defined analogously.' With '$Y'_k = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_i$' (p. 144) and '$Y'_{1k} = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_{1i}$ and $Y'_{0k} = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_{0i}$' (p. 145). The sums over clusters run over $k = 1,\ldots,M$.

(S8) Section 6.4, p. 145 (PDF p. 11): 'Our goal is now to derive conservative variance estimators: although not unbiased, these estimators are guaranteed to have a nonnegative bias.' Footnote 7: 'Although the variance estimator is nonnegatively biased, the associated standard errors may not be (due to Jensen's inequality) and any particular draw may be above or below the true value of the variance due to sampling variability.'

Reading conventions used in every target below (they follow from (S1)-(S7) in the two-arm case that the paper works in; stated here for the formalizer and flagged as conventions, not quotations): the assignment vector $(T_1,\ldots,T_N)$ has an arbitrary probability distribution on $\{0,1\}^N$ (a finite sample space), and all expectations, variances and covariances are taken over it; every unit is assigned to treatment or control, so $\pi_{1i} = \Pr(T_i = 1)$, $\pi_{0i} = \Pr(T_i = 0) = 1 - \pi_{1i}$, $\pi_{1i1j} = \Pr(T_i = 1, T_j = 1)$, $\pi_{0i0j} = \Pr(T_i = 0, T_j = 0)$, $\pi_{1i0j} = \Pr(T_i = 1, T_j = 0)$, hence $\pi_{1i1i} = \pi_{1i}$, $\pi_{0i0i} = \pi_{0i}$ and $\pi_{1i0i} = 0$, and likewise for the primed cluster quantities; the clusters $K_1,\ldots,K_M$ partition $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, $T_i = T'_k$ for every $i \in K_k$, and distinct clusters have distinct indicators, $\Pr(T'_k \neq T'_l) > 0$ for $k \neq l$; every double sum over $k, l$ (or $i, j$) is over ordered pairs; 'the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever' means $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$ for every unit $i$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.1, the second option for deriving theta_i while preserving unbiasedness, with footnote 5; as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. p. 142 (PDF p. 8), Section 5.1: 'Following the basic logic of Williams [44], a second option, only possible in some studies, is to exploit the fact that for some units $i,j$, $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j$. Recall from (1) that $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$, where $Y_{1i}$ and $Y_{0i}$ are constants. Since the only stochastic component of $Y_i$ is $T_i$, then $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j$, and $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp Y_j$. If $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ is a function of any or all of the elements of the set $\{Y_j : T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j\}$ and no other random variables, then $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \theta_{\mathbf{i}}$. It follows that $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ and therefore $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.' Footnote 5 (p. 142): 'More formally and without loss of generality, let $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}) = f(\mathbf{X_i},g(\mathbf{Z},Y_j)) = f(\mathbf{X_i},g(\mathbf{Z},h(Y_{0j},Y_{1j},T_j)))$, where $\mathbf{Z}$ is a matrix of pretreatment covariates (that may or may not coincide with $\mathbf{X_j}$), $g(.)$ is an arbitrary function (e.g., the least squares fit), and $h(.)$ is the function implied by eq. [1]. Since only $T_j$ is a random variable, the random variable $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ equals some function $f'(T_j)$. $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j$ implies $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp f'(T_j)$ (equivalently $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$) which, in turn, implies $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.' The passage continues (p. 142): 'There are many studies where this option is available. Consider first an experiment where units are independently assigned to treatment. Without loss of generality, let us assume that the analyst chooses $f(.)$ to be linear. The analyst can then derive a parameter vector $\theta_i$ for each unit $i$ in the following way: for each $i$, the analyst could perform an ordinary least squares regression of the outcome on covariates for all units except for unit $i$. Another example where the second option could be used is a block-randomized experiment. In a block-randomized experiment, units are partitioned into multiple groups, with randomization only occurring within partitions. Since the treatment assignment processes in different partitions are independent, $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j$ for all $i,j$ such that $i$ and $j$ are in separate blocks. To derive $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ for each $i$, the analyst could then use a regression of outcomes on covariates including all units not in unit $i$'s block.'

Formal content of the general rule as printed: for a unit $i$, if $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ is a deterministic function of the observed outcomes $Y_j$ of units $j$ each of which satisfies $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp T_j$ (pairwise), then $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp \theta_{\mathbf{i}}$, $T_i \perp\!\!\!\perp f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). Generalized difference estimator: eqs. [13]-[14], p. 140 (PDF p. 6), $\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$ and $\widehat{Y_0^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-T_i)\frac{Y_{0i}}{\pi_{0i}} - (1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$, 'where $f(.)$ is a predetermined real-valued function of pretreatment covariate vector $\mathbf{X_i}$ and of parameter vector $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$'; eq. [15], p. 141 (PDF p. 7), $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} - \widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right)$; eq. [16], p. 141, $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$. Sufficient condition (p. 141, PDF p. 7): 'As we prove in Appendix B, a sufficient condition for $\widehat{\Delta_G}$ to be unbiased is that, for all $i$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.' Section 5.1 opens (p. 142): 'Consider two ways that one might derive $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ that satisfy $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$. The simplest is to assign a fixed value to $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$, so that $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ has no variance, and thus no covariance with $T_i$.'
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, for a finding rated Moderate. The general rule is false (P026-T4); it is true when the set contains a single unit, when $T_i$ is independent of the whole vector of assignments used (P026-T5(a)), and for additive predictions (P026-T5(d)). The two examples quoted at the end are correct (P026-T5(e)). The first option (a fixed $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$) is not touched.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Eqs. [5]-[8]: unbiasedness of the Horvitz-Thompson estimators of the totals and of the ATE
canonical_claim.statement:
Under the standing assumptions ('We assume that, $\forall i$, $\pi_{1i} > 0$ and $\pi_{0i} > 0$', p. 138): 'Define the Horvitz-Thompson estimator [20] of $Y_1^T$, $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_{1i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_i$ [6] and, similarly, define the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of $Y_0^T$, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_i$. [7] The estimators in eqs. [6] and [7] are unbiased for $Y_1^T$ and $Y_0^T$, respectively, since $\mathrm{E}[T_i] = \pi_{1i}$ and $\mathrm{E}[1 - T_i] = 1 - \pi_{1i} = \pi_{0i}$. From eq. [4], it follows that we may construct an unbiased estimator of $\Delta$: $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} - \widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}Y_iT_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}Y_i(1-T_i)\right]$. [8] We refer to this estimator of the ATE as the HT estimator.' With eq. [5] (p. 138): $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_1^T}] - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_0^T}]\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right] = \Delta$. And (p. 139, Section 4.1): 'The HT estimator is unbiased for all designs'.

That is: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}}] = Y_1^T$, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}] = Y_0^T$ and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_{HT}}] = \Delta$ for every assignment distribution with $\pi_{1i} > 0$ and $\pi_{0i} > 0$ for all $i$, whatever the dependence between the $T_i$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). Eq. [4], p. 138: $\widehat{\Delta} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y_1^T} - \widehat{Y_0^T}\right]$. Bias and unbiasedness: p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S2).
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statement. The second equalities in eqs. [6] and [7] ($T_iY_{1i} = T_iY_i$ and $(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = (1-T_i)Y_i$) are identities from eq. [1].

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4.1, eqs. [11] and [12]: the HT estimator under complete random assignment of units (difference in means) and of clusters
canonical_claim.statement:
(a) Section 4.1.1: 'Consider a design where a fixed number of units ($n$ out of $N$) is selected for inclusion in the treatment, each with equal probability $n/N$. The associated estimator is $\widehat{\Delta_{DM}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{N}{n}Y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{N}{N-n}Y_i\right] = \frac{\sum_{i\in I_1}Y_i}{n} - \frac{\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i}{N-n}$. [11]' and (p. 140) 'Eq. [11] shows that for the special case where $n$ of $N$ units are selected into treatment, the HT estimator reduces to the difference-in-means estimator: the average outcome among treatment units minus the average outcome among control units.'
(b) Section 4.1.2: 'Consider a design where a fixed number of clusters ($m$ out of $M$ clusters) is selected for inclusion in the treatment, each with equal probability $m/M$. The associated estimator is $\widehat{\Delta_{C}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{M}{m}Y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{M}{M-m}Y_i\right] = \frac{M}{N}\left[\frac{\sum_{i\in I_1}Y_i}{m} - \frac{\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i}{M-m}\right]$. [12] Contrast the estimator in eq. [12] with the estimator in eq. [11]. A key insight is that eq. [12] does not reduce to the difference-in-means estimator in eq. [11]. In fact, the difference-in-means estimator may be biased for cluster randomized experiments [5].'

Formal content. (a) If every assignment of positive probability has exactly $n$ treated units, $0 < n < N$, and $\pi_{1i} = n/N$, $\pi_{0i} = (N-n)/N$ for all $i$, then on every such assignment $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in I_1}Y_i - \frac{1}{N-n}\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i$, where $I_1 = \{i : T_i = 1\}$ and $I_0 = \{i : T_i = 0\}$; so the difference in means is unbiased for $\Delta$ in this design. (b) If the units are partitioned into $M$ clusters assigned as wholes and $\pi_{1i} = m/M$, $\pi_{0i} = (M-m)/M$ for all $i$, $0 < m < M$, then $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{M}{N}\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i\in I_1}Y_i - \frac{1}{M-m}\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i\right]$, which is unbiased for $\Delta$. (c) There is a design of type (b) in which the difference-in-means estimator $\frac{\sum_{i\in I_1}Y_i}{|I_1|} - \frac{\sum_{i\in I_0}Y_i}{|I_0|}$ is biased for $\Delta$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). HT estimator: eqs. [6]-[8], p. 139 (PDF p. 5), $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_{1i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_i$, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_i$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} - \widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}Y_iT_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}Y_i(1-T_i)\right]$. The index sets $I_1$ and $I_0$ are not defined in the paper; they are the sets of units assigned to treatment and to control (the text calls the right side of eq. [11] 'the average outcome among treatment units minus the average outcome among control units'). In eq. [12], $N$ is the number of units and $M$ the number of clusters.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statement. For (c) the paper gives no example (it cites [5]); a witness, computed when this target was fixed and not taken from the paper: three clusters of sizes 1, 1, 2, exactly one cluster treated with probability 1/3 each, $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$ equal to $1$, $1$, $0$, $0$ for the four units, so $\Delta = 0$; the difference in means takes the values $2/3$, $2/3$, $-1$ (expectation $1/9$), while eq. [12] takes the values $3/8$, $3/8$, $-3/4$ (expectation $0$). The rest of headline claim H2 (bias of IPW and regression estimators) is carried by the numerical example of Section 7 and is not a formal statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix B (eqs. [39]-[40]) with eqs. [13]-[16]: the generalized difference estimator is unbiased when Cov(T_i, f(X_i, theta_i)) = 0 for all i
canonical_claim.location: Appendix B, p. 150 (PDF p. 16); pp. 140-141 (PDF pp. 6-7)
canonical_claim.statement:
p. 141: 'As we prove in Appendix B, a sufficient condition for $\widehat{\Delta_G}$ to be unbiased is that, for all $i$, $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.' Appendix B, p. 150: 'Assume that $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$, for all $i \in (1,2,\ldots,N)$. $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y_1^{T*}}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}}\right] - \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}}\right] + \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\pi_{1i}Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{1i}\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}}\right] + \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{E}[f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})] = Y_1^T - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{E}[f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})] + \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{E}[f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})] = Y_1^T$ [39] and, likewise, $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right] = Y_0^T$. [40] The third line of eq. [39] follows from $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$. The key insight is that, if $\mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$, the two right-most terms in eqs. [13] and [14] cancel in expectation and, therefore, the terms do not lead to bias in the estimation of $Y_1^T$ or $Y_0^T$.'

That is: under the standing assumptions, for real-valued random variables $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ on the assignment space with $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$ for every $i$: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_1^{T*}}] = Y_1^T$, $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_0^{T*}}] = Y_0^T$ and hence (eqs. [5], [15]) $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_G}] = \Delta$. In particular this holds when each $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ is constant across randomizations (p. 142: 'The simplest is to assign a fixed value to $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$, so that $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ has no variance, and thus no covariance with $T_i$.'). Also the identity eq. [16], valid for every assignment: $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). HT estimator: eqs. [6]-[8], p. 139 (PDF p. 5), $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_{1i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_i$, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_i$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} - \widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}Y_iT_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}Y_i(1-T_i)\right]$. Eqs. [13]-[15], pp. 140-141: $\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$; $\widehat{Y_0^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-T_i)\frac{Y_{0i}}{\pi_{0i}} - (1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$; $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} - \widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right)$. Eq. [5], p. 138: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_1^T}] - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_0^T}]\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right] = \Delta$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statement; it holds as printed. The companion bias identity for general (randomization-dependent) $f$ is P026-T13, and the data-derived route to the zero-covariance condition is P026-T4, P026-T5 and P026-T18. In eq. [40] the condition used is $\mathrm{Cov}(1 - T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = -\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})) = 0$.
